sentences.text: Learned counsel for the applicant submits that the trial Court has erroneously acquitted the respondents, although, there was sufficient evidence warranting their conviction.

He submits that the applicant had entered into an agreement to sell on 15.02.2008 with respondent No. 1 for the plot measuring 500 sq. yards which was in the name of the firm owned by respondent No.1 Varinder Patel and one Manmeet Mishra for a total sale consideration of 14,00,000.
He had paid 4,00,000 as earnest money to respondent No. 1 and the last date for executing the agreement to sell was fixed for 15.05.2008.
However, respondent No.1 did not get the agreement executed and made flimsy excuses for delay in its execution.
He also submits that respondent No.1 instead had sold the land to respondent no 2 Gursewak Singh on 16.07.2010 and they colluded with each other to defraud the applicant.

He further submits that the Trial Court has erred in finding that all the pages of the agreement to sell running into 6 pages were not signed by respondent No.1 and it only bore his signatures on the last page.

3. Heard.
4.

The applicant is stated to have entered into an agreement to sell with respondent no1 on 15.02.2008 for the land measuring 500 sq. yds situated in village Bhamian Kalan, Abadi Sarian Colony, Tehsil and District Ludhiana for a total sale consideration of Rs. 14 lakhs.
He has stated to have 2 of 6 Neutral Citation No:=2025:PHHC:001865-DB CRM-A-302-2021 (O&M) paid the earnest money amounting to 4 lakhs to respondent No.1 on 15.02.2008.

5. It is manifest that the criminal complaint had been filed by the applicant before police only on 04.02.2011, though the agreement to sell is stated to have been entered into on 15.02.2008 and the last date for execution was 15.05.2008.
The respondent No.1 is stated to have sold the land to respondent No.2 on 16.07.2010, almost 2 years after the expiry of last date fixed for execution of the agreement to sell with the applicant.

The applicant had filed a suit for specific performance,
which was later dismissed in default.

He did not take any steps for restoration of the suit and instead after several years, he filed the criminal complaint against the respondents which appears to be an afterthought and the dispute which was primarily civil in nature, was sought to be converted into criminal one.
It is apparent that the origin of the dispute is with regard to the specific performance of the Agreement to Sell.
The applicant has not been able to produce any evidence to indicate that the respondents had the intention to deceive the applicant from the very inception.
The applicant also did not issue any notice to respondent No.1 for execution and registration of the agreement to sell.
He has also not produced on record any evidence to prove his bona fides with regard to execution of agreement to sell and payment of balance sale consideration.
In recent times, there is a growing tendency to launch criminal proceedings in disputes which are patently civil in nature.

Reference can be made to the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of 3 of 6 Neutral Citation No:=2025:PHHC:001865-DB CRM-A-302-2021 (O&M) Naresh Kumar and another Versus The State Karnataka, 2024 INSC 196, wherein the Supreme Court had held that mere breach of contract by any party would not attract criminal prosecution.

In Usha Chakraborty & Anr. v. State of West Bengal & Anr. 2023 SCC OnLine SC 90, relying upon Paramjeet Batra (supra) it was again held that where a dispute which is essentially of a civil nature, is given a cloak of a criminal offence,
then such disputes can be quashed, by exercising the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

entities.text: Usha Chakraborty & Anr. v. State of West Bengal & Anr. 2023 SCC OnLine SC 90
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Essentially, the present dispute between the parties relates to a breach of contract.

A mere breach of contract, by one of the parties, would not attract prosecution for criminal offence in every case, as held by this Court in Sarabjit Kaur v. State of Punjab and Anr. (2023) 5 SCC 360.

entities.text: Sarabjit Kaur v. State of Punjab and Anr. (2023) 5 SCC 360
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Similarly, dealing with the distinction between the offence of cheating and a mere breach of contractual obligations,
this Court, in Vesa Holdings (P) Ltd. v. State of Kerala, (2015) 8 SCC 293, has held that every breach of contract would not give rise to the offence of cheating, and it is required to be shown that the accused had fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise.

6. Consequently, we do not find any illegality in the judgment of the trial Court acquitting the respondents.
It is trite that interference in an appeal against acquittal would be warranted where the judgment is perverse or manifestly illegal.
By the judgment of acquittal, the presumption of innocence of the accused is reinforced.
Even if, another view is possible from appreciation of evidence, the appellate Court would refrain from interfering in an order of acquittal.
Reference may be made to the judgment of the Supreme Court in Chandrappa & Ors vs State Of Karnataka, 2007 4 of 6 Neutral Citation No:=2025:PHHC:001865-DB CRM-A-302-2021 (O&M) (4) SCC 415.

sentences.text: An appellate Court, however, must bear in mind that in case of acquittal, there is double presumption in favour of the accused.

Firstly, the presumption of innocence available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent court of law.
Secondly, the accused having secured his acquittal, the presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court.
(5) If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record, the appellate court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial court.

"xxx xxx the following general principles regarding powers of appellate Court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal emerge;
(1) An appellate Court has full power to review, reappreciate and reconsider the evidence upon which the order of acquittal is founded;
(2) The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 puts no limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such power and an appellate Court on the evidence before it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of fact and of law;
(3) Various expressions, such as, 'substantial and compelling reasons', 'good and sufficient grounds', 'very strong circumstances', 'distorted conclusions', 'glaring mistakes', etc. are not intended to curtail extensive powers of an appellate Court in an appeal against acquittal.
Such phraseologies are more in the nature of 'flourishes of language' to emphasize the reluctance of an appellate Court to interfere with acquittal than to curtail the power of the Court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion.
